array-map.title: Array mapping
array-map.description: Transform each array element with a function to produce a new array.

javascript.explanation: Use the built-in map method to transform an array.
javascript.designRationale: JavaScript's map method is central to functional programming, returning a new array without modifying the original.

python.explanation: Use a list comprehension to transform an array.
python.designRationale: Python list comprehensions are the most Pythonic approach and are more intuitive than map.

go.explanation: Go has no built-in map function; implement the transformation explicitly with a for loop.
go.designRationale: Go emphasizes explicitness and simplicity, avoiding excessive abstraction.

rust.explanation: Use the iterator map method and collect to gather the results.
rust.designRationale: Rust iterators are zero-cost abstractions, with the same compiled performance as handwritten loops.

ruby.explanation: Use map with a block to transform the elements.
ruby.designRationale: Ruby block syntax makes higher-order function calls natural and elegant.

php.explanation: Use the built-in array_map function with an arrow function to transform an array.
php.designRationale: Arrow functions in PHP 7.4+ make callbacks more compact; array_map returns a new array without modifying the original.
pros: Preserves keys for a single array

cpp.explanation: Use std::transform with a lambda to map each element of a container.
cpp.designRationale: STL algorithms with lambdas are the modern approach since C++11 and allow extensive compiler optimization.
pros: Works with any container or iterator
cons: Requires preallocating the target container or using back_inserter

error-handling.title: Error handling
error-handling.description: Handle operations that may fail and make callers explicitly address failure paths.

javascript.explanation: JavaScript commonly uses try/catch to catch exceptions thrown synchronously or within async/await.
javascript.designRationale: The exception model keeps the normal path short, but failures must be handled explicitly at call boundaries.

go.explanation: Go returns error as an ordinary value; callers must check it explicitly and preserve context.
go.designRationale: Explicit error returns put failure paths in the control flow, emphasizing readability and contextual wrapping.

rust.explanation: Rust uses Result<T, E> to represent success values and failure reasons in the type system; ? propagates errors.
rust.designRationale: Result exposes potentially failing functions in their signatures, so callers cannot ignore the failure branch.

java.explanation: Java represents failures with exceptions, releases resources with try-with-resources, and exposes failure boundaries with throws.
java.designRationale: Checked exceptions bring some failure paths into method signatures, while resource-management syntax reduces missed close operations.

php.explanation: PHP uses throw and try/catch to express exceptional paths; typed exceptions allow precise catching.
php.designRationale: Throwing exceptions for unrecoverable situations or violated preconditions avoids mixing success and failure in return values.

string-interpolation.title: String interpolation
string-interpolation.description: Embed variable or expression values in strings without sacrificing readability through scattered concatenation.

javascript.explanation: JavaScript uses template literals and ${...} to embed variables or expressions.
javascript.output: Hello, Alice! You are 30 years old.
javascript.designRationale: Template literals put text and expressions in one literal, making them more suitable than concatenation for text with multiple variables.

python.explanation: Python uses f-strings to embed variables and expressions in strings.
python.output: Hello, Alice! You are 30 years old.
python.designRationale: f-strings are the most direct string-formatting approach in Python 3, with clear expression placement.

go.explanation: Go has no built-in string interpolation syntax; fmt.Sprintf is commonly used for formatting.
go.output: Hello, Alice! You are 30 years old.
go.designRationale: Go chooses explicit formatting functions to clarify formatting controls and their correspondence with parameter types.
cons: Placeholder and argument order must be kept in sync manually

swift.explanation: Swift uses \(...) to insert variables or expressions into strings.
swift.output: Hello, Alice! You are 30 years old.
swift.designRationale: Swift interpolation combines with strongly typed expressions to keep UI text and debugging output readable.

array-filter.title: Array filtering
array-filter.description: Filter array elements by a condition and return a new array of matching elements.

javascript.explanation: Use filter to select even numbers.
javascript.designRationale: filter returns a new array and preserves the original, following functional programming principles.

python.explanation: Use a list comprehension with a conditional expression to filter elements.
python.designRationale: List comprehensions are Python's most idiomatic filtering approach.

rust.explanation: Use the iterator filter method to select elements.
rust.designRationale: Rust iterators provide zero-cost abstractions, with the same compiled performance as handwritten loops.

kotlin.explanation: Use the higher-order filter function with a lambda expression.
kotlin.designRationale: Kotlin collection operators are concise and type-safe.

php.explanation: array_filter selects elements by a predicate; array_values resets numeric indices.
php.designRationale: array_filter preserves original keys by default; combine it with array_values when contiguous indices are needed.
cons: Preserving keys by default can cause surprises

cpp.explanation: Use std::copy_if with back_inserter to append matching elements to the target container.
cpp.designRationale: C++20 ranges also allow numbers | views::filter(...), a more declarative form.

pattern-matching.title: Pattern matching
pattern-matching.description: Branch on the structure and contents of a value.

rust.explanation: Use a match expression to pattern-match an enum.
rust.designRationale: Rust pattern matching is exhaustive; the compiler ensures all cases are handled.

swift.explanation: Use a switch statement to pattern-match an enum.
swift.designRationale: Swift switch must cover all cases, providing compile-time safety guarantees.

python.designRationale: Python pattern matching provides more powerful branching.

null-safety.title: Null safety
null-safety.description: Safely handle potentially absent values to avoid null pointer exceptions.

rust.explanation: Use Option to explicitly represent a value that may be absent.
rust.designRationale: Rust has no null; Option requires handling the absent-value case.

kotlin.explanation: Use nullable types and the safe-call operator.
kotlin.designRationale: Kotlin's type system distinguishes nullable and non-nullable types, providing compile-time null safety.

swift.explanation: Use Optional and if let binding.
swift.designRationale: Swift's Optional type provides compile-time null-safety guarantees.

typescript.explanation: Use a union type to represent a value that may be null.
typescript.designRationale: TypeScript's strict null-checking mode provides compile-time null safety.

async-await.title: Async/await
async-await.description: Express asynchronous flows in a form close to sequential code, avoiding deeply nested callbacks.

javascript.explanation: JavaScript uses async to declare a function returning a Promise and await to pause until the Promise settles.
javascript.designRationale: async/await rewrites Promise chains into control structures closer to synchronous flows.

python.explanation: Python uses async def to define a coroutine and await to wait for another coroutine or awaitable to complete.
python.designRationale: asyncio lets high-latency I/O share an event loop; asyncio.run connects it to synchronous code at the entry point.
cons: Cannot freely nest asyncio.run within an existing event loop

csharp.explanation: C# uses async Task<T> to express an asynchronous return value and await to wait for the Task to complete.
csharp.designRationale: The Task model gives asynchronous operations types; async/await combines naturally with exception propagation and generic return values.

swift.explanation: Swift uses async throws to mark functions that are asynchronous and may fail; try await expresses both waiting and error propagation.
swift.designRationale: Swift puts both asynchrony and errors in function signatures, making waiting and failure points clear to callers.
pros: Combines naturally with throws error handling

destructuring.title: Destructuring assignment
destructuring.description: Extract values from arrays or objects and assign them to variables.

javascript.explanation: Use object and array destructuring syntax.
javascript.designRationale: Destructuring makes code more concise and avoids repeated property access.

python.explanation: Use tuple unpacking and extended unpacking.
python.designRationale: Python unpacking syntax is concise and intuitive, and is a core language feature.

rust.explanation: Use struct and slice pattern matching.
rust.designRationale: Rust pattern matching provides powerful destructuring.

closure.title: Closures
closure.description: Create anonymous functions that can capture outer variables.

javascript.explanation: A closure captures the outer count variable to create private state.
javascript.designRationale: JavaScript closures are a core mechanism for data encapsulation and modularity.

python.explanation: Use nonlocal to modify an outer variable.
python.designRationale: Python closures need a nonlocal declaration to modify outer variables.

rust.explanation: Use move to transfer ownership into the closure.
rust.designRationale: Rust closures follow ownership rules to ensure memory safety.

swift.designRationale: Swift closures have concise syntax and automatically manage captured variables.

php.explanation: PHP closures explicitly capture outer variables with use; & captures by reference.
php.designRationale: Explicit use clarifies capture semantics and avoids unintentionally carrying extensive context.

cpp.explanation: A lambda captures by value with [count]; mutable allows the captured copy to be modified.
cpp.designRationale: C++ lambdas explicitly control capture by value or reference to avoid dangling references.
pros: Can be inlined by the compiler

iterator-pattern.title: Iterator pattern
iterator-pattern.description: Traverse collection elements without exposing their internal representation.

python.explanation: Implement __iter__ and __next__ to create an iterator.
python.designRationale: Python's iterator protocol allows objects to be used in for loops.

rust.designRationale: Rust iterators are zero-cost abstractions with a rich set of combinators.

java.explanation: Implement the Iterable and Iterator interfaces.
java.designRationale: Java's iterator pattern is central to its collections framework.

cpp.explanation: STL containers expose a common begin()/end() interface; range-for is syntactic sugar for it.
cpp.designRationale: Iterators are the core STL abstraction decoupling containers from algorithms.
pros: Supports random-access, bidirectional, and forward categories

decorator-pattern.title: Decorator pattern
decorator-pattern.description: Dynamically add responsibilities or functionality to an object.

python.designRationale: Python decorators are syntactic sugar that makes code more concise and elegant.
pros: Does not intrude on original code

typescript.designRationale: TypeScript decorators provide metaprogramming capabilities, commonly used in framework development.

java.explanation: Implement a decorator by wrapping an object.
java.designRationale: Java uses interfaces and composition to implement the decorator pattern.

immutability.title: Immutability
immutability.description: Create data structures that cannot be modified to avoid side effects.

javascript.explanation: Use spread syntax to create new objects and arrays.
javascript.designRationale: Immutability makes code more predictable and easier to debug and test.

rust.explanation: Rust is immutable by default; mut must be declared explicitly.
rust.designRationale: Rust is immutable by default, encouraging safe programming practices.

kotlin.explanation: Use the copy method of a data class to create a modified copy.
kotlin.designRationale: Kotlin data classes provide convenient operations on immutable data.

method-chaining.title: Method chaining
method-chaining.description: Call multiple methods in sequence, with each method returning the object itself.

javascript.explanation: Array methods return new arrays, allowing method chaining.
javascript.designRationale: Method chaining clarifies data transformation flows and makes code more expressive.

python.explanation: Each method returns self to enable chaining.
python.designRationale: The Builder pattern constructs complex objects through method chaining.

rust.explanation: Iterator methods return new iterators, allowing method chaining.
rust.designRationale: Rust iterator chains are zero-cost abstractions.

php.explanation: Each method returns $this; a self type hint helps the IDE infer the return type correctly.
php.designRationale: Laravel's Eloquent / Query Builder exemplifies this pattern.

dependency-injection.title: Dependency injection
dependency-injection.description: Pass dependencies in from outside rather than creating them internally.

typescript.designRationale: Dependency injection makes code easier to test and maintain.

java.designRationale: Java DI frameworks such as Spring widely use this pattern.

python.designRationale: Python duck typing makes DI more flexible.

lazy-evaluation.title: Lazy evaluation
lazy-evaluation.description: Delay computation until its result is actually needed.

python.explanation: Use a generator for lazy evaluation.
python.designRationale: Generators produce values on demand, saving memory.

rust.explanation: Iterator chains are lazy and execute only when collect is called.
rust.designRationale: Rust iterators are lazy by default, improving performance.

javascript.explanation: Use a generator function for lazy evaluation.

builder-pattern.title: Builder pattern
builder-pattern.description: Build complex objects step by step using a fluent interface.

java.explanation: Use an inner Builder class to construct immutable objects.
java.designRationale: The Builder pattern suits objects with many optional parameters.

rust.explanation: Use a Builder struct and method chaining.
rust.designRationale: Rust's Builder pattern uses the ownership system to ensure type safety.

typescript.explanation: Use a Builder class and method chaining.
typescript.designRationale: TypeScript's Builder pattern provides type-safe object construction.

cpp.explanation: Return *this for chained configuration; build() && restricts the call to an rvalue context to ensure a single consumption.
cpp.designRationale: C++ has no named parameters; Builder makes construction of multi-field objects more readable.

memoization.title: Memoization
memoization.description: Cache function results to avoid repeated computation.

javascript.explanation: Use Map to cache function results.
javascript.designRationale: Memoization reduces exponential time complexity to linear.

python.designRationale: The Python standard library provides an efficient LRU cache implementation.

rust.designRationale: Rust requires explicit cache management but provides zero-cost abstractions.

pipeline-pattern.title: Pipeline pattern
pipeline-pattern.description: Process data through a series of transformation functions.

javascript.explanation: Use reduce to implement a function pipeline.
javascript.designRationale: The pipeline pattern makes data transformation flows clear and readable.

rust.explanation: Use trait extension methods to implement a pipeline.
rust.designRationale: Rust's trait system supports elegant method chaining.

python.explanation: Use reduce and lambda to implement a pipeline.
python.designRationale: Python's functional features support the pipeline pattern.

observer-pattern.title: Observer pattern
observer-pattern.description: Define a one-to-many dependency between objects and notify all observers when an object changes state.

javascript.designRationale: JavaScript's event-driven model widely uses the observer pattern.

java.explanation: Use interfaces to implement the observer pattern.
java.designRationale: Java's observer pattern is a classic implementation of a GoF design pattern.

python.explanation: Use classes to implement the observer pattern.
python.output:
Observer 1 Received: Hello
Observer 2 Received: Hello
python.designRationale: Python duck typing makes the observer pattern more flexible.

php.explanation: Constrain observers with an interface; the subject keeps a list of observers and broadcasts events.
php.designRationale: The PHP standard library also provides SplSubject/SplObserver, but custom interfaces often offer more control.

singleton-pattern.title: Singleton pattern
singleton-pattern.description: Ensure a class has only one instance and provide a global access point.

javascript.explanation: Store the sole instance in a static property.
javascript.designRationale: JavaScript singletons are implemented through closures or static properties.

java.explanation: Use double-checked locking to implement a thread-safe singleton.
java.designRationale: Java singletons must account for thread safety and lazy initialization.

python.designRationale: Python singletons can be implemented with __new__ or decorators.

rust.explanation: Use lazy_static and Mutex to implement a thread-safe singleton.
rust.designRationale: Rust singletons must account for ownership and thread safety.

php.explanation: A private constructor and a static method provide a single instance; ??= simplifies first-time initialization.
php.designRationale: A traditional singleton suffices in PHP's single-process model; modern practice favors management through a dependency injection container.
cons: Difficult to replace with mocks, making testing harder

cpp.explanation: Meyers Singleton: a function-local static variable guarantees thread-safe lazy initialization since C++11.
cpp.designRationale: Disabling copy construction and assignment prevents accidental copies of the singleton.
cons: Destruction order is difficult to control

recursion.title: Recursion
recursion.description: Solve a problem by having a function call itself.

javascript.explanation: Use recursion to calculate a factorial.
javascript.designRationale: Recursion breaks a problem into smaller subproblems.

python.explanation: Use recursion to calculate a factorial.
python.designRationale: Python limits recursion depth; stack overflow must be considered.

rust.designRationale: Rust recursion can be optimized by the compiler into tail recursion.

go.explanation: Use recursion to calculate a factorial.
go.designRationale: Go supports recursion but does not perform tail-call optimization.

cpp.explanation: Classic recursive factorial; the compiler can optimize tail-recursive cases into loops when optimization is enabled.
cpp.designRationale: C++ does not guarantee tail-call optimization; deep recursion still risks stack overflow.
pros: Code closely follows the mathematical definition

javascript.description: A lightweight, interpreted programming language used primarily for web development.

typescript.description: A superset of JavaScript that adds a static type system.

python.description: A high-level, general-purpose programming language that emphasizes code readability.

go.description: A statically typed, compiled language developed by Google, focused on simplicity and concurrency.

rust.description: A systems programming language focused on safety, concurrency, and performance.

java.description: A widely used object-oriented programming language that emphasizes cross-platform portability.

csharp.description: A modern object-oriented programming language developed by Microsoft for the .NET platform.

ruby.description: A dynamic, open-source programming language focused on simplicity and productivity.

php.description: A server-side scripting language widely used for web development.

swift.description: A modern programming language developed by Apple for iOS and macOS development.

kotlin.description: A modern programming language developed by JetBrains, fully interoperable with Java.

cpp.description: A high-performance, general-purpose programming language supporting low-level memory operations.

inheritance.title: Class inheritance and composition
inheritance.description: Compare subclass reuse and overriding; where class inheritance is absent, show alternative structures such as composition.
inheritance.scopeNote: Compares native mechanisms and alternatives in this catalog; a mechanism being inapplicable does not mean that object-oriented programming or code reuse is unsupported.

javascript.summary: Classes use extends to establish superclass and prototype relationships; subclasses can define their own methods.
javascript.versionNotes: The baseline is ECMAScript 2023, citing the fixed-version specification. The generics entry shows runtime-generic methods, not static type parameters.

typescript.summary: extends creates a subclass inheriting superclass members; TypeScript also checks the declared types.
typescript.versionNotes: The baseline is TypeScript 5.3, and the selected syntax is compatible with it. Sources use the continuously updated official Handbook; closures cite the older official Functions chapter. Static contracts must be distinguished from runtime behavior.

python.summary: A subclass specifies its base class in its definition and can override methods; Python also supports multiple base classes.
python.versionNotes: The baseline is Python 3.12; the def keep[T] syntax in the example requires 3.12. Protocol comes from the standard library, and type annotations are generally checked by external type-checking tools.

ruby.summary: A subclass specifies its superclass with <, can override inherited methods, and can call the superclass implementation with super.
ruby.versionNotes: The baseline is Ruby 3.2, citing the corresponding official documentation. The generics entry demonstrates reuse with dynamic collections, not static type parameter declarations.

java.summary: A class inherits one superclass through extends and can override instance methods that permit overriding.
java.versionNotes: Based on the Java 21 JLS. All snippets use syntax supported by this baseline; this does not imply that the features were introduced in Java 21.

csharp.summary: A class has only one direct base class; virtual methods allow derived classes to override them with override.
csharp.versionNotes: C# 12 is the compatibility baseline. Microsoft Learn documentation is continuously updated; no newer-version or preview syntax is used.

kotlin.summary: Classes and members are final by default; open permits inheritance or overriding, and override explicitly overrides a member.
kotlin.versionNotes: Kotlin 1.9 is the compatibility baseline. The official documentation is continuously updated; JVM-default compiler options from later versions are not used.

php.summary: A class inherits one superclass through extends and can override eligible inherited public or protected methods, excluding final methods.
php.versionNotes: PHP 8.3 is the compatibility baseline; later features such as PHP 8.4 interface properties are not used. The absence of native generics is established from the type system and type declaration documentation, not inferred solely from examples.

go.summary: There is no class inheritance or type inheritance hierarchy. Composition and embedding commonly provide behavior reuse; methods and interfaces still support object-oriented design.
go.versionNotes: The specification is pinned to go1.21.0. Independent method type parameters, range over integers or functions, and Go 1.22 loop-variable semantics are excluded.

rust.summary: A struct cannot inherit the fields and methods of another struct. Composition and trait default methods commonly provide code reuse; methods and visibility can still encapsulate data.
rust.versionNotes: The baseline is Rust 1.75, edition 2021. The current official Rust Book was consulted; entries use only features already supported in 1.75, excluding edition 2024 changes and later APIs. The web tool could not read the version 1.75 book URL.

cpp.summary: A class can derive from one or more base classes; access specifiers control accessibility.
cpp.versionNotes: Based on the C++20 N4861 working draft, checked against the source at the n4861 tag in the cplusplus/draft repository. The HTML transcription is used only to locate clauses. The working draft is not the officially published ISO standard; later features from the latest draft are excluded.

swift.summary: A class can inherit one superclass and explicitly override members with override; structs and enums do not participate in class inheritance.
swift.versionNotes: The baseline is Swift 5.9. The current official Swift language book source was consulted; examples use only features already supported in 5.9, excluding later Swift 6 concurrency or ownership extensions. Because the web page body requires JavaScript, the official swiftlang/swift-book source was read instead.

polymorphism.title: Polymorphism and behavioral contracts
polymorphism.description: Use the same call with different implementations: distinguish interfaces, protocols, traits, and dynamic duck typing.
polymorphism.scopeNote: Compares native mechanisms and alternatives in this catalog; a mechanism being inapplicable does not mean that object-oriented programming or code reuse is unsupported.

javascript.summary: Callers invoke same-named object methods by convention for runtime polymorphism; this demonstrates a dynamic protocol, not a static interface declaration.
javascript.versionNotes: The baseline is ECMAScript 2023, citing the fixed-version specification. The generics entry shows runtime-generic methods, not static type parameters.

typescript.summary: interface describes a static contract, and implements checks whether a class satisfies it; this clause does not change type inference for methods in the class.
typescript.versionNotes: The baseline is TypeScript 5.3, and the selected syntax is compatible with it. Sources use the continuously updated official Handbook; closures cite the older official Functions chapter. Static contracts must be distinguished from runtime behavior.

python.summary: The standard-library typing.Protocol describes structural contracts for static checking; ordinary type annotations do not enforce method signatures at runtime.
python.versionNotes: The baseline is Python 3.12; the def keep[T] syntax in the example requires 3.12. Protocol comes from the standard library, and type annotations are generally checked by external type-checking tools.

ruby.summary: Callers invoke same-named methods by convention for duck-typed polymorphism; a module can share method implementations but is not a static interface contract.
ruby.versionNotes: The baseline is Ruby 3.2, citing the corresponding official documentation. The generics entry demonstrates reuse with dynamic collections, not static type parameter declarations.

java.summary: Classes explicitly implement interface contracts, allowing types to follow the same contract without inheriting the same application-specific base class.
java.versionNotes: Based on the Java 21 JLS. All snippets use syntax supported by this baseline; this does not imply that the features were introduced in Java 21.

csharp.summary: Both class and struct can implement multiple interface contracts.
csharp.versionNotes: C# 12 is the compatibility baseline. Microsoft Learn documentation is continuously updated; no newer-version or preview syntax is used.

kotlin.summary: A class can implement multiple interfaces; interfaces can provide method implementations but cannot store instance state.
kotlin.versionNotes: Kotlin 1.9 is the compatibility baseline. The official documentation is continuously updated; JVM-default compiler options from later versions are not used.

php.summary: A class explicitly implements one or more interfaces with implements, fulfilling their shared contracts through public methods.
php.versionNotes: PHP 8.3 is the compatibility baseline; later features such as PHP 8.4 interface properties are not used. The absence of native generics is established from the type system and type declaration documentation, not inferred solely from examples.

go.summary: Interface values support dynamic method dispatch; a concrete type implicitly implements an interface when it has the required method set.
go.versionNotes: The specification is pinned to go1.21.0. Independent method type parameters, range over integers or functions, and Go 1.22 loop-variable semantics are excluded.

rust.summary: A trait defines shared behavior. Generic trait bounds support static dispatch; for suitable traits, references such as &dyn Trait support runtime dispatch.
rust.versionNotes: The baseline is Rust 1.75, edition 2021. The current official Rust Book was consulted; entries use only features already supported in 1.75, excluding edition 2024 changes and later APIs. The web tool could not read the version 1.75 book URL.

cpp.summary: Virtual functions support dynamic dispatch. An abstract class with pure virtual functions can express an interface without a separate interface keyword.
cpp.versionNotes: Based on the C++20 N4861 working draft, checked against the source at the n4861 tag in the cplusplus/draft repository. The HTML transcription is used only to locate clauses. The working draft is not the officially published ISO standard; later features from the latest draft are excluded.

swift.summary: Protocols declare requirements that types must satisfy; classes, structs, and enums can conform. Protocol extensions can provide reusable implementations.
swift.versionNotes: The baseline is Swift 5.9. The current official Swift language book source was consulted; examples use only features already supported in 5.9, excluding later Swift 6 concurrency or ownership extensions. Because the web page body requires JavaScript, the official swiftlang/swift-book source was read instead.

generics.title: Generics and type parameters
generics.description: Compare generic mechanisms that preserve type relationships and the limits of value reuse in dynamic languages.
generics.scopeNote: Compares native mechanisms and alternatives in this catalog; a mechanism being inapplicable does not mean that object-oriented programming or code reuse is unsupported.

javascript.summary: Generic reuse here means runtime-generic algorithms: Array.prototype.map can be applied to array-like objects, rather than declaring static type parameters.
javascript.versionNotes: The baseline is ECMAScript 2023, citing the fixed-version specification. The generics entry shows runtime-generic methods, not static type parameters.

typescript.summary: Type parameters relate input and output types, allowing the same function to work with multiple types.
typescript.versionNotes: The baseline is TypeScript 5.3, and the selected syntax is compatible with it. Sources use the continuously updated official Handbook; closures cite the older official Functions chapter. Static contracts must be distinguished from runtime behavior.

python.summary: Python 3.12 type parameter syntax can declare generic functions; type relationships in annotations are checked by type tools, not enforced on runtime arguments.
python.versionNotes: The baseline is Python 3.12; the def keep[T] syntax in the example requires 3.12. Protocol comes from the standard library, and type annotations are generally checked by external type-checking tools.

ruby.summary: Runtime collection algorithms can be reused with different object types: Array can contain elements of different types, and map calls a block for each element. This is not a static type parameter declaration.
ruby.versionNotes: The baseline is Ruby 3.2, citing the corresponding official documentation. The generics entry demonstrates reuse with dynamic collections, not static type parameter declarations.

java.summary: Classes and methods can declare type parameters; different parameterizations of the same generic class share a runtime class.
java.versionNotes: Based on the Java 21 JLS. All snippets use syntax supported by this baseline; this does not imply that the features were introduced in Java 21.

csharp.summary: Type parameters support statically checked generic code and retain runtime type information.
csharp.versionNotes: C# 12 is the compatibility baseline. Microsoft Learn documentation is continuously updated; no newer-version or preview syntax is used.

kotlin.summary: Classes and functions support type parameters; in and out express declaration-site variance.
kotlin.versionNotes: Kotlin 1.9 is the compatibility baseline. The official documentation is continuously updated; JVM-default compiler options from later versions are not used.

php.summary: PHP 8.3 does not support native parameterized generics. The mixed example only demonstrates dynamic reuse; it does not express a generic constraint requiring the input and return value to have the same type. PHPDoc static-analysis annotations are also outside the native type system.
php.versionNotes: PHP 8.3 is the compatibility baseline; later features such as PHP 8.4 interface properties are not used. The absence of native generics is established from the type system and type declaration documentation, not inferred solely from examples.

go.summary: Functions and types can declare constrained type parameters. Go 1.21 methods cannot declare additional independent type parameters.
go.versionNotes: The specification is pinned to go1.21.0. Independent method type parameters, range over integers or functions, and Go 1.22 loop-variable semantics are excluded.

rust.summary: Functions, structs, and other constructs can use type parameters; trait bounds specify the operations a type must provide.
rust.versionNotes: The baseline is Rust 1.75, edition 2021. The current official Rust Book was consulted; entries use only features already supported in 1.75, excluding edition 2024 changes and later APIs. The web tool could not read the version 1.75 book URL.

cpp.summary: Templates define families of related functions or types; C++20 also supports constraints and concepts.
cpp.versionNotes: Based on the C++20 N4861 working draft, checked against the source at the n4861 tag in the cplusplus/draft repository. The HTML transcription is used only to locate clauses. The working draft is not the officially published ISO standard; later features from the latest draft are excluded.

swift.summary: Generic functions and types use type parameters and can constrain them to specify required behavior.
swift.versionNotes: The baseline is Swift 5.9. The current official Swift language book source was consulted; examples use only features already supported in 5.9, excluding later Swift 6 concurrency or ownership extensions. Because the web page body requires JavaScript, the official swiftlang/swift-book source was read instead.

closures.title: Closures and captures
closures.description: Functions carry their defining environment; compare capture, mutation of outer variables, and lifetime constraints.
closures.scopeNote: Compares the same concept across the 12 languages in this catalog; semantics and constraints are not necessarily identical.

javascript.summary: Function expressions retain their lexical environment at definition time; outer parameters remain accessible after the outer call returns.
javascript.versionNotes: The baseline is ECMAScript 2023, citing the fixed-version specification. The generics entry shows runtime-generic methods, not static type parameters.

typescript.summary: As in JavaScript, functions can capture variables from outer scopes; type annotations provide static descriptions.
typescript.versionNotes: The baseline is TypeScript 5.3, and the selected syntax is compatible with it. Sources use the continuously updated official Handbook; closures cite the older official Functions chapter. Static contracts must be distinguished from runtime behavior.

python.summary: Nested functions and lambdas can reference variables from an outer scope.
python.versionNotes: The baseline is Python 3.12; the def keep[T] syntax in the example requires 3.12. Protocol comes from the standard library, and type annotations are generally checked by external type-checking tools.

ruby.summary: A Proc object retains the context in which it was created; a lambda can use local variables from its enclosing method.
ruby.versionNotes: The baseline is Ruby 3.2, citing the corresponding official documentation. The generics entry demonstrates reuse with dynamic collections, not static type parameter declarations.

java.summary: A lambda targets a functional interface; captured local variables must be final or effectively final.
